rationale: Stored solutions [2,0] cannot be achieved with any single-constant edit to the original system y=x-1 and y=x^2-3x+1. Setting equal always yields x^2-4x+(c+1)=0, whose roots always sum to 4; roots {0,2} would require sum 2 — impossible without changing the x-coefficient of the quadratic, which is a second edit. Therefore the fallback path is taken: change the quadratic's constant term from +1 to +2 (one character). This gives x^2-4x+3=0=(x-1)(x-3), solutions x=1 and x=3 — clean integers, appropriate GCSE difficulty, discriminant 4 (perfect square). new_solutions updated to [1,3].

new_misconceptions.message: When you move the quadratic to the other side, remember to move EVERY term — the constant \(-1\) on the left must cross to the right too; otherwise you get \(x^2 - 4x + 2 = 0\) instead of \(x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0\) and land on irrational answers.

With \(x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0\), you need two numbers that multiply to \(+3\) and add to \(-4\); those are \(-1\) and \(-3\), so the brackets are \((x - 1)(x - 3) = 0\) — don't let the negative signs slip when you write the factors.

Setting the equations equal means \(x - 1 = x^2 - 3x + 2\); move everything to one side by subtracting \((x - 1)\) from both sides, not adding it — otherwise you get \(x^2 - 2x + 1 = 0\), which only gives the one solution \(x = 1\) and misses \(x = 3\).

Take care with the constants when you rearrange: the \(-1\) on the left moves to give \(+1\) on the right, so \(2 + 1 = 3\) giving \(x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0\) — writing \(+4\) by mistake produces the perfect square \((x - 2)^2 = 0\), which has only one answer.
